learner:
Level: strong Python (classes, dicts, asyncio); no experience with compiled languages or static typing.
Goal: write production Rust from zero.
Known gaps: understands shared references in Python; guessed move semantics correctly but with low confidence; has never seen a borrow checker.

lessons.title: What a compiler does for you
lessons.objective: Explain how running a Rust program differs from running a Python script, and when errors are caught.
lessons.hook: Rust's biggest promise is that whole classes of bugs never reach production; that starts with compiling.
lessons.aside: Rust compiles through LLVM, the same backend used by Clang for C and C++.
lessons.explain: Python reads your .py file and runs it through an interpreter every time. Rust works differently. A compiler translates your whole program into a machine-code binary before it runs. Rust catches type and memory errors at compile time, before the program ever runs. Example: in Python, passing a string where a number is expected only fails when that line executes, maybe weeks later in production. In Rust, the same mistake stops the build, so the bug never ships. The compiled binary runs without needing Rust installed on the target machine.
key_facts: A compiler translates your whole program into a machine-code binary before it runs.
Rust catches type and memory errors at compile time, before the program ever runs.
The compiled binary runs without needing Rust installed on the target machine.

predict.q: A Rust function is called with a string where it expects a number, on a line that rarely runs. When is this reported?

angles: Think of the compiler as a strict reviewer who reads every line before anything runs. Python's interpreter is a reviewer who reads each line only as it is about to execute.
Shipping a Rust program means shipping one finished binary. Shipping a Python program means shipping source code plus an interpreter to run it.
claims: Rust compiles programs to machine code before execution.
Rust detects type errors at compile time.
A compiled Rust binary does not require the Rust toolchain on the machine that runs it.

misconceptions: Rust detects type errors at runtime, as Python does

items.why: The binary is already machine code and does not need the Rust toolchain.
misconceptions: The compiler is needed at runtime, like an interpreter
Cargo acts as a runtime launcher
Binaries are tied to the build machine's Rust install

items.answer: At compile time, before the program runs.
items.why: Rust catches type and memory errors at compile time, before the program ever runs.

items.answer: Nothing Rust-specific; the binary runs on its own.

lessons.title: Creating and running a project with Cargo
lessons.objective: Create, run, and release-build a Rust project with Cargo.
lessons.hook: Cargo is the one tool you use for building, running, testing, and managing dependencies.
lessons.explain: Cargo is Rust's build tool and package manager. `cargo new hello` creates a project with Cargo.toml and src/main.rs. Inside main.rs is `fn main()`, which is where the program starts. `cargo run` compiles the project and then runs the binary. Cargo.toml lists dependencies, similar to requirements.txt or pyproject.toml in Python. Example: add `rand = "0.8"` under [dependencies], and the next `cargo run` downloads and builds it. For production, `cargo build --release` produces an optimized binary in target/release.
key_facts: `cargo new hello` creates a project with Cargo.toml and src/main.rs.
`cargo run` compiles the project and then runs the binary.
Cargo.toml lists dependencies, similar to requirements.txt or pyproject.toml in Python.
`cargo build --release` produces an optimized binary in target/release.

lessons.title: Immutable by default
lessons.objective: Declare immutable and mutable variables and use shadowing correctly.
lessons.hook: In Python any name can be reassigned; Rust makes you state when something changes, which makes code easier to reason about.
lessons.explain: Variables in Rust are immutable by default. `let x = 5; x = 6;` is a compile error. Adding `mut` (`let mut x`) allows a variable to be reassigned: `let mut count = 0; count += 1;` works. Rust also lets you write `let` again with the same name. Shadowing with a new `let` creates a new variable with the same name, and it may have a different type. Example: `let input = "42"; let input: i32 = input.parse().unwrap();` turns text into a number while reusing the name. With `mut`, by contrast, you can change the value but never the type.
key_facts: Variables in Rust are immutable by default.
Adding `mut` (`let mut x`) allows a variable to be reassigned.
Shadowing with a new `let` creates a new variable with the same name, and it may have a different type.
angles: Treat `let` like defining a constant-ish name. To change it, either opt in with `mut` or make a fresh name with another `let`.
`mut` changes the value in the same box. Shadowing throws away the old box and makes a new one with the same label, which can hold a different type.
claims: Rust variables are immutable unless declared with mut.
Reassigning an immutable variable is a compile error.
Shadowing allows a new variable with a different type under the same name.

items.q: By default, a Rust variable declared with `let` is:
items.why: Rust variables are immutable unless marked mut.
misconceptions: Rust behaves like Python's reassignable names

items.q: Which line lets `count` be incremented later?
items.why: mut goes right after let to make the binding mutable.
misconceptions: mut is part of the type annotation

items.q: `let s = "7"; let s: i32 = s.parse().unwrap();` compiles because:
options: The second let shadows with a new type
items.answer: The second let shadows with a new type
items.why: Shadowing creates a new variable that may have a different type.

items.q: `let mut v = "hi"; v = 3;` fails. Why?
options: mut allows new values, not a new type
mut was placed in the wrong spot
items.answer: mut allows new values, not a new type
items.why: mut permits reassignment only with the same type; changing type needs shadowing.

items.q: What keyword makes a Rust variable reassignable?
items.why: Adding mut allows a variable to be reassigned.

items.why: Shadowing with a new let creates a new variable that may have a different type.

lessons.title: Static types and inference
lessons.objective: Read and write type annotations, rely on inference, and convert number types explicitly.
lessons.hook: Types are how the compiler catches bugs early; knowing the rules removes most early compile errors.
lessons.explain: Every Rust value has a type fixed at compile time. Python type hints are optional and not enforced at runtime, but Rust types are always enforced. You rarely have to write them. Rust usually infers types, so `let x = 5;` gives x the type i32. You can annotate when you want: `let big: i64 = 5;`. Rust never converts between number types implicitly; you write `as` or use a conversion method. Example: `x + big` fails to compile because i32 and i64 differ, while `x as i64 + big` works.
key_facts: Every Rust value has a type fixed at compile time.
Rust usually infers types, so `let x = 5;` gives x the type i32.
Rust never converts between number types implicitly; you write `as` or use a conversion method.

predict.q: `let a: i32 = 1; let b: i64 = 2; let c = a + b;` What happens?

angles: Imagine mypy running in strict mode on every build, with no way to skip it. That's close to Rust's type checker, but stricter about numbers.
Inference means the compiler writes the annotation for you; it doesn't mean the type can change later.

Integer literals default to i32.
Rust has no implicit numeric conversions.

items.why: Integer literals default to i32 when nothing else constrains them.

items.q: How do you add an i32 `a` to an i64 `b`?
items.why: Rust requires an explicit conversion between number types.

items.why: Every value's type is fixed at compile time, whether written or inferred.

items.why: Every Rust value has a type fixed at compile time.

lessons.title: Functions and expression-based returns
lessons.objective: Write annotated functions that return values with a final expression.
lessons.hook: A single stray semicolon is the most common beginner compile error in Rust functions.
lessons.explain: Function parameters and return types must be annotated, as in `fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32`. Unlike in Python, the compiler won't infer them from the function body. Rust is expression-based. The last expression in a block, written without a semicolon, is the block's value. So `fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }` returns the sum with no `return`. Adding a semicolon turns an expression into a statement, which evaluates to `()`. Example: writing `a + b;` makes the body return `()`, the empty unit type, and the compiler reports a mismatch with i32. Use `return` only for early exits.
key_facts: Function parameters and return types must be annotated, as in `fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32`.
The last expression in a block, written without a semicolon, is the block's value.
Adding a semicolon turns an expression into a statement, which evaluates to `()`.
angles: Read the final line without a semicolon as an implicit `return`. Adding the semicolon throws the value away.
`()` is Rust's 'nothing' value, similar in role to a Python function that falls off the end and returns None, except Rust checks that against the declared return type.
claims: Rust function parameters require type annotations.
A block's final expression without a semicolon is its value.
A statement evaluates to the unit type ().

items.q: Which function signature is valid Rust?
items.why: Parameters and return types must be annotated with Rust syntax.

items.q: What does `fn f() -> i32 { 3 + 4 }` return?
items.why: The final expression without a semicolon is the function's value.

items.q: Why does `fn f() -> i32 { 3 + 4; }` fail?
items.why: A semicolon turns the expression into a statement that yields ().
misconceptions: Literals cannot be used in arithmetic

items.q: What is the value of `let y = { let x = 2; x * 10 };`?
items.why: Any block's last expression without a semicolon is the block's value.
misconceptions: Blocks cannot be used as values

items.q: What value does a statement ending in a semicolon evaluate to?
items.why: Adding a semicolon makes a statement, which evaluates to ().

items.q: How do you return a value from a Rust function without the return keyword?
items.answer: Write it as the last expression in the body with no semicolon.
accept: leave off the semicolon on the last line
items.why: The block's final expression without a semicolon is its value.

lessons.title: Stack, heap, and String
lessons.objective: Explain where i32 and String data live, and distinguish String from &str.
lessons.hook: Ownership rules exist because of heap data; this is the mental model they rest on.
lessons.explain: Python stores nearly everything as heap objects and hides this from you. Rust makes it visible. Values with a size known at compile time, like i32, can live on the stack, which is fast and freed automatically. A `String` stores its text on the heap and keeps a pointer, length, and capacity on the stack. That lets it grow: `let mut s = String::from("hi"); s.push_str("!");`. A literal like `"hi"` has type &str. `&str` is a borrowed view of string data, while `String` owns its text and can grow. Example: a function that only reads text can take &str; one that builds text returns String.
key_facts: Values with a size known at compile time, like i32, can live on the stack.
A `String` stores its text on the heap and keeps a pointer, length, and capacity on the stack.
`&str` is a borrowed view of string data, while `String` owns its text and can grow.

angles: Picture a String as a small ticket on the stack (pointer, length, capacity) that points to the real characters stored on the heap.
&str is like looking at text through a window you don't own. String is owning the text yourself, so you can add to it.

lessons.title: Ownership and moves
lessons.objective: Predict when a value is moved, which variables remain usable, and when memory is freed.
lessons.hook: Ownership is how Rust frees memory with no garbage collector; it shows up in almost every line you write.
lessons.explain: Each value in Rust has exactly one owner. In Python `b = a` makes two names share one object; in Rust `let b = a;` with a String transfers it instead. Assigning a String to another variable moves ownership, and the original variable can no longer be used. Example: `let a = String::from("hi"); let b = a; println!("{}", a);` fails with 'borrow of moved value: a'. Only b owns the heap text now. Rust needs no garbage collector because of one rule: when the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory is freed. Here that happens to b at the closing `}`.
key_facts: Each value in Rust has exactly one owner.
Assigning a String to another variable moves ownership, and the original variable can no longer be used.
When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory is freed.
In Python `b = a` makes two names share one object; in Rust `let b = a;` with a String transfers it instead.
fixes: Believes `let b = a;` makes both names share the String, as Python name binding does
Unsure whether the original variable is still usable after a move

predict.q: `let a = String::from("hi"); let b = a; println!("{}", a);` What happens?

angles: Ownership is like handing over a physical key: after `let b = a;`, b holds the key and a's hand is empty. The compiler won't let you use an empty hand.
If both a and b owned the heap text, both would try to free it at the end of scope. Moving makes sure only one owner frees it.
claims: Every Rust value has one owner.
Assigning a String moves it and invalidates the source variable.
Values are dropped when their owner goes out of scope.
Python assignment binds another name to the same object.

items.q: After `let b = a;` where a is a String, what is true?
options: a and b share the String
a and b each own a copy
a owns it, b borrows it
items.why: Assignment transfers ownership of a String rather than sharing it like Python.
misconceptions: Rust assignment works like Python name binding

items.q: After `let b = a;` (a String), what does using `a` do?
items.why: The original variable can no longer be used after a move.
misconceptions: Moves leave an empty value behind

items.q: When is a String's heap memory freed?
options: When its owner goes out of scope
items.answer: When its owner goes out of scope
items.why: Values are dropped when their owner leaves scope.
misconceptions: Rust uses manual memory management like C

items.q: How many owners can a single String value have at once?
items.why: Each value in Rust has exactly one owner.
misconceptions: Ownership starts when a value is used

items.q: In Python, `b = a` binds two names to one object. What does `let b = a;` do with a String in Rust?
items.answer: It moves ownership to b, and a can no longer be used.
items.why: In Rust, let b = a; with a String transfers it instead of sharing.

items.q: What happens to a value when its owner goes out of scope?
items.answer: It is dropped and its memory is freed.
items.why: When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory is freed.

lessons.title: Copy types and clone
lessons.objective: Tell which types are copied versus moved, and use clone deliberately.
lessons.hook: Knowing why integers don't move but Strings do removes most of the confusion about moves.
lessons.explain: Not everything moves. Types that implement `Copy`, like i32, bool, and char, are copied on assignment instead of moved. So `let x = 5; let y = x;` leaves both usable. String is not `Copy` because copying it would require duplicating heap data, which can be expensive and should be visible in code. When you really want two independent Strings, ask for it: `.clone()` makes an explicit deep copy of a String, so both variables stay usable. Example: `let a = String::from("hi"); let b = a.clone();` lets you print both a and b.
key_facts: Types that implement `Copy`, like i32, bool, and char, are copied on assignment instead of moved.
`.clone()` makes an explicit deep copy of a String, so both variables stay usable.
String is not `Copy` because copying it would require duplicating heap data.

predict.q: `let x = 5; let y = x; println!("{}", x);` What happens?

angles: Small fixed-size values are cheap to duplicate, so Rust copies them silently. Heap values could be large, so duplicating them requires you to write clone.
Seeing `.clone()` in code is a signal that a real allocation happens there, which is useful when you review code for performance.
claims: i32, bool, and char implement Copy.
Copy types are duplicated on assignment.
clone performs a deep copy of a String.
String does not implement Copy.

items.q: Which type is moved, not copied, on assignment?
items.why: String owns heap data and is not Copy.

items.q: After `let b = a.clone();` with a String a, which is true?
options: Both a and b are usable
items.answer: Both a and b are usable
items.why: clone makes an independent deep copy.

items.q: Why isn't String a Copy type?
items.why: Implicit copies would hide potentially expensive heap allocations.

items.q: `let c = 'x'; let d = c;` Is c still usable?
items.why: char implements Copy, so assignment copies it.

items.q: Which method makes an explicit deep copy of a String?
items.why: .clone() makes an explicit deep copy so both variables stay usable.

items.q: Name two types that are copied rather than moved on assignment.
items.why: Types implementing Copy, like i32, bool, and char, are copied.

lessons.title: Borrowing with references
lessons.objective: Pass values to functions by reference so callers keep ownership, and mutate through &mut.
lessons.hook: Borrowing lets you use data without giving it away, which is how most real Rust functions take their arguments.
lessons.explain: Passing a String by value to a function moves it into the function. After `print_it(s)`, s is gone, just like after `let b = s;`. A reference `&s` lets code use a value without taking ownership. A function that takes `&String` or `&str` borrows the value, and the caller keeps ownership. Example: `fn len(s: &str) -> usize { s.len() }` called as `len(&name)` leaves name usable afterward. To modify something, borrow it mutably. `&mut s` is a mutable reference that allows changing the borrowed value; s must be declared `mut`: `fn shout(s: &mut String) { s.push('!'); }`.
key_facts: A reference `&s` lets code use a value without taking ownership.
Passing a String by value to a function moves it into the function.
A function that takes `&String` or `&str` borrows the value, and the caller keeps ownership.
`&mut s` is a mutable reference that allows changing the borrowed value; s must be declared `mut`.
fixes: Expects a String to stay usable after passing it to a function by value

predict.q: `fn take(s: String) {}` then `take(name); println!("{}", name);` What happens?

angles: Passing by value is giving someone your book. Passing &book is letting them read it at your desk. Passing &mut book is letting them write in it while you wait.
Function arguments follow the same rules as `let`: a plain String argument moves, and an & argument borrows.
claims: References allow access without taking ownership.
Passing a String by value moves it into the function.
Borrowing parameters leave ownership with the caller.
Mutable references require the original variable to be mut.

items.why: A borrowed parameter leaves ownership with the caller.

items.q: What does `&s` give you?
items.why: A reference borrows a value without owning it.

items.q: `let s = String::new(); add(&mut s);` fails. Why?

lessons.title: The borrow checker's rules
lessons.objective: Read borrow checker errors and restructure code to satisfy the shared-or-mutable rule.
lessons.hook: These rules are the source of Rust's main safety guarantee, and also of most beginner frustration.
lessons.aside: Modern Rust uses non-lexical lifetimes, so a borrow ends at its last use rather than at the end of the block.
lessons.explain: The borrow checker is the part of the compiler that enforces reference rules. Python lets any number of names mutate a list at the same time. Rust forbids this. At any moment you can have either any number of shared references `&T` or exactly one mutable reference `&mut T`. Example: `let r = &v; v.push(4); println!("{:?}", r);` fails because push needs `&mut v` while r is still in use. Also, a reference cannot outlive the value it points to, so returning `&` to a local variable is rejected. These rules prevent data races and dangling pointers at compile time.
key_facts: The borrow checker is the part of the compiler that enforces reference rules.
At any moment you can have either any number of shared references `&T` or exactly one mutable reference `&mut T`.
A reference cannot outlive the value it points to.
These rules prevent data races and dangling pointers at compile time.
fixes: Assumes, as in Python, that many names can mutate the same value at once

predict.q: `let r = &v; v.push(4); println!("{:?}", r);` What happens?
options: Compile error: v is already borrowed

angles: Think of a document with readers and one editor: many readers at once, or one editor alone, never both. That way no reader sees a half-edited page.
Pushing to a Vec may move its buffer to a new heap location. A reader holding the old address would then point to freed memory, which is exactly what the rule prevents.
claims: The borrow checker is part of the Rust compiler.
Rust allows many shared references or one mutable reference at a time.
References cannot outlive their referents.
Borrow rules prevent data races and dangling pointers at compile time.

items.q: Which combination of borrows of v can be active at the same time?
items.why: Any number of shared references, or exactly one mutable reference, may be active.
misconceptions: Multiple mutable aliases are fine, as in Python
Readers and a writer can coexist

items.why: Only one mutable reference may exist at a time.
misconceptions: Rust silently clones for each borrow

items.q: Why is `fn f() -> &String { let s = String::new(); &s }` rejected?
items.why: A reference cannot outlive the value it points to.

items.q: What do the borrow rules prevent at compile time?
items.why: Enforcing shared-xor-mutable and lifetimes rules out these bugs.
misconceptions: Borrow rules check arithmetic and performance

items.q: State the borrow rule about shared and mutable references.
items.answer: At any moment, either any number of shared references (&T) or exactly one mutable reference (&mut T).
items.why: That rule is what the borrow checker enforces.

items.q: What part of the compiler enforces reference rules?
items.why: The borrow checker enforces reference rules.
